analysis.one_liner: Lets student borrowers refinance federal consolidation loans and choose their own loan company.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 85 cosponsors from both parties but died in a House committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal student loan rules then barred borrowers from refinancing a consolidation loan to catch a lower rate, and steered them to a single lender. This bill would have repealed that refinancing ban, let borrowers pick their own consolidator, capped new loan interest rates at 6.8 percent, limited origination fees to 0.5 percent, and required lenders and schools to give borrowers clear disclosures about rates, repayment plans, and prepayment.
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers with federal loans, who could refinance at a lower fixed rate instead of being locked into whatever rate applied when they first consolidated, choose among competing lenders, and pay no more than a 0.5 percent origination fee.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the prohibition on refinancing consolidation loans, so borrowers could reconsolidate to capture a lower interest rate [S2][S3].
Removes the rules that tied a borrower to a particular lender for consolidation, letting students choose their consolidator [S2][S3].

Caps interest rates on new federal student loans and consolidation loans made after July 1, 2006 at 6.8 percent (7.5 percent for PLUS parent loans), set annually from the 91-day Treasury bill rate plus 2.3 percent [S3].

Limits origination fees on consolidation loans to 0.5 percent of principal and requires lenders and schools to give borrowers clear notices about rates, repayment plans, total interest, and prepayment rights [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Student loan lenders and consolidators, who would lose the guaranteed stream of consolidation business and the higher interest rates that came from borrowers being unable to refinance or shop around.

drawbacks.text: Capping rates at 6.8 percent and limiting fees would shrink lender margins in the federally guaranteed loan program; lenders argued that lower margins could reduce their willingness to lend, and guarantee agencies would bear added subsidy costs from repeated refinancing at market rates [S3].
Allowing repeated reconsolidation whenever rates fall adds administrative cost to the federal loan system, since each refinancing must be re-underwritten and re-guaranteed [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers the bill offered a direct, tangible benefit: a chance to trade a high fixed rate for a lower one and to pick a lender rather than be assigned one. The costs fall on lenders and, indirectly, on the federal subsidy accounts that compensate them. The main design question is that frequent refinancing tied to short-term Treasury rates adds administrative churn to the loan system.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Wu introduced the bill on March 1, 2005, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
On March 24, 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on 21st Century Competitiveness, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill attracted 85 cosponsors, 76 Democrats and 9 Republicans, but the committee never acted on it before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders and consolidators, who kept their locked-in consolidation business and their protection from borrower refinancing because the bill never advanced. Borrowers got no relief from the higher rates the bill would have addressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan lenders kept their consolidation business

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought broader support.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Boehner (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (76 of 85) with modest Republican support (9), and the Republican-run committee never brought the bill up.

industries.industry: Federal student loan lenders and consolidators (FFEL program lenders)
industries.note: The bill would have let borrowers refinance their loans and shop among lenders, breaking the lock that kept consolidation business with whichever lender a borrower was routed to. It also capped rates and fees, cutting lender revenue on every loan.
Schools would take on a new disclosure duty for students considering consolidation. The burden is administrative and small.
